turns.content: Hey, so I did something last night that’s been sitting weirdly with me this morning. Clare told me she’s staying at Julian’s on Friday instead of our movie night, and I just said “Cool, have fun,” then went to bed. Do you think that came off as passive-aggressive? I’m trying to figure out if I’m overthinking this.

I can't tell you whether it came off as passive-aggressive — that depends on how Clare heard it, which isn't in what you've described.

What the evidence supports: you said five words, "Cool, have fun," and went to bed. That's the observable event. Whether it read as passive-aggressive depends on tone, timing, and context you haven't given — did you say it flatly or normally, was there a pause, had you two already discussed Friday, and did you have a reaction you didn't voice?

Two things worth separating:

1. **What you felt.** You said it's "sitting weirdly." That's a report about you, not evidence about Clare's interpretation.
2. **What Clare likely heard.** Unknown. The most direct way to settle it is to ask her, or to say what you actually felt — e.g., "I said 'cool, have fun' last night but I was a bit disappointed about Friday. I'm not upset at you, I just noticed it."

If your real question is whether you *were* being passive-aggressive: saying a neutral phrase while suppressing a feeling isn't automatically passive-aggressive. It becomes that when the phrase is meant to convey the unspoken feeling as a message. Only you know which it was.

If you want, tell me what you were actually feeling when you said it, and I can help you figure out what — if anything — is worth saying to her.

Hmm, I think you're right that it depends on tone and context. I said it pretty flatly, not mean, but also not warm. Do you think that's worth bringing up to her, or would that make it more awkward than just letting it go?

Both options are defensible; the deciding factor is whether the flatness was a one-off or a pattern.

**Case for letting it go:** one flat "Cool, have fun" is a single data point. If you were tired, or it was late, or you genuinely didn't mind, there's nothing to repair. Raising it can create a problem Clare didn't experience.

**Case for bringing it up:** if you *were* disappointed and said the flat thing instead of the real thing, that's the part worth addressing — not the tone, but the gap between what you felt and what you said. Left alone, that gap tends to repeat, and repeated flatness around her plans is what reads as a message over time.

If you bring it up, keep it about you and short:

> "Last night I said 'cool, have fun' but I was actually a little bummed about Friday. Not a big deal — I just didn't want to pretend I wasn't."

That's not awkward because it doesn't ask her to account for anything. It just corrects the record.

What I'd avoid: asking her "did that come off passive-aggressive?" That puts her in the position of either reassuring you or confirming a criticism, and neither is useful.

One thing I don't know: whether Friday movie night is a standing thing you both count on, or a casual plan. If it's standing and she's changing it, that's a different conversation than if it was loose to begin with.

Yeah, I think you're right that bringing it up would be about the gap, not the tone. It's a standing thing—we've done Friday movie night pretty much every week since she moved in. Do you think I should text her now, or wait until we see each other tonight?

Wait until tonight, unless there's a reason you can't.

Reasons for in person: this is about a standing weekly ritual between two people who live together, and the content is "I was a little disappointed." That lands better with tone and face than in text, where flatness is exactly the thing that gets misread — the same problem you're trying to fix.

Reasons a text could be fine: if you won't see her tonight, or if you'd otherwise sit on it and let it build. A short text is better than stewing.

If you do text, keep it to the same two sentences and don't open a thread:

> "Hey — last night I said 'cool, have fun' but I was actually a little bummed about Friday. Not a big deal, just didn't want to pretend I wasn't."

One thing worth deciding before tonight: what you actually want. Two different asks hide behind "I was bummed":

- **You want the ritual protected** — e.g., "Friday's kind of our thing; can we keep it or move it?" That's a request, and she can say no.
- **You just want to have said it** — no ask, just not pretending. That's the version above.

Those lead to different conversations. If it's the first, say the request out loud instead of hoping she infers it from the disappointment.

What about if I just tell her tonight, "Hey, I realized my 'cool have fun' last night sounded flat and I didn't mean it that way"... is that too much? Or should I just stick with the honest version about being a little bummed?

Stick with the honest version. The "I didn't mean it that way" framing has a problem: it isn't true to what you told me. You said you were flat *and* that you were a little bummed. Saying "I didn't mean it that way" walks back the flatness as an accident, when the flatness was the tell.

It also invites the wrong reply. "I didn't mean it that way" asks Clare to accept a correction and move on. "I was actually a little bummed" tells her something real and lets her respond to that.

So:

> "Last night I said 'cool, have fun' but I was actually a little bummed about Friday. Not a big deal — I just didn't want to pretend I wasn't."

That's not too much. It's two sentences, it's about you, and it doesn't ask her to justify anything.

The only thing to add is the piece from your last message: if Friday movie night is a standing weekly thing and you want it kept or moved, say that too — as a request, not a hint. Something like "Friday's kind of our thing — can we keep it, or pick another night?" She can say no, and that's a real answer you'd want.

Okay, that makes sense. So just two sentences tonight, honest and about me, no walking it back. But what if she asks why I was bummed... do I say it's because Friday is our thing, or do I keep it vague?

Say the real reason. "Friday is our thing" is the real reason — it's not vague, it's specific and it's yours.

If she asks, something like:

> "Because Friday's been our thing since you moved in. I look forward to it. I'm not saying you can't go to Julian's — I just noticed I was disappointed."

That does three things: names the reason, states it as your feeling rather than her fault, and pre-empts the thing she might otherwise hear ("you're not allowed to go"). If you leave it vague, she'll fill the gap herself, and the likely fill is worse than the truth.

Two things to be ready for, since they're the realistic branches:

- **She offers to change her plans.** You don't have to accept. "No, go — I just wanted you to know" is a complete answer. Accepting out of guilt would make the conversation a transaction instead of a disclosure.
- **She says it's just one Friday, or that it's not a big deal to her.** That's information, not a rebuttal. It may mean the ritual matters more to you than to her. That's worth knowing and worth a separate conversation about whether Friday stays a standing thing — but not one to force tonight.

What you're not doing: asking her to account for going, or making Julian's part of it. Keep it on the two of you and the Friday habit.
